To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) inner wall surface contamination of ionization chambers with a thin layer (0.01 mm) of a material with atomic number Z>20 can result in an over-response to photons of energy less than 0.5 MeV that is not predicted by the percentage composition in the chamber, and (2) the over-response can be as high as 50%.

the over-response of an ionization-chamber to low-energy photons is greatly underestimated by a calculation of the percentage composition of a thin layer of high-Z material on the chamber inner wall, and that the over-response can be significant for low-energy units that have been calibrated with such a chamber.

(1) the inner wall surface of an ionization-chamber can be contaminated with a thin high-Z layer which produces an over-response to photons of energy less than 50 keV and (2) the over-response is not predictable from knowledge of the total percentage composition of the high-Z material in the entire chamber, as is commonly assumed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method to measure the dose rate of the low-energy photons emitted by the 125I seeds used for radiation therapy.
the development of a new type of radiation detector for the measurement of low-energy photons.
the effect of high-Z contamination of the surface of an ionization-chamber on its response to low-energy x-rays.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the over-response of tissue-equivalents to low-energy photons can be significant and that the effect can be minimized by using a thin layer of high-Z contaminant.

the over-response of an ionization-chamber at low energies due to a thin layer of high-Z contamination of the inner wall is a function of the energy and the composition of the photon beam, the energy and thickness of the contaminant, and the geometry of the chamber.
the use of a tissue-equivalent ion chamber contaminated with a high-Z material for the calibration of a low-energy unit is not recommended.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for low-energy units with a high-Z contaminant on the chamber wall, a factor of 2 or more is needed to convert the measured exposure to the dose to tissue at 1 meter from the source.
the use of a contaminated chamber for calibration of a low-energy unit will result in a calibration factor which is too large.

a thin layer of a relatively high-Z material on an inner surface of an ionization-chamber wall can produce a large over-response to low energies, which is greatly underestimated from the percentage composition of that contaminant in the chamber.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the calibration of low-energy x-ray units should be performed with chambers having inner surfaces of low-Z materials.
the calibration of a low-energy unit should not be performed with a chamber contaminated by high-Z materials.
the calibration of low-energy units should not be performed with a contaminated ionization chamber, and that the use of contaminated chambers should be avoided in general.
